candidate_facts_list.fact: dbt Core v1.2 introduced a `grants` config for resources
candidate_facts_list.quote: In v1.2, we introduced a `grants` config

candidate_facts_list.fact: `grants` is configured as a structured dictionary (e.g., {'select': ['role']}); dbt chooses the most efficient path to apply them
candidate_facts_list.quote:
You configure `grants` as a structured dictionary rather than writing all the SQL yourself
* dbt will take *the most efficient path* to apply those grants

candidate_facts_list.fact: If `grants` is missing or set to {} dbt will not manage grants for that table
candidate_facts_list.quote: if `grants` is missing or set to `{{}}`, dbt will understand that you don’t want it managing grants for this table.

candidate_facts_list.fact: When changing grants, dbt computes diffs and can issue REVOKE statements (visible in debug-level logs)
candidate_facts_list.quote: you should see ... dbt has run a `revoke` statement.

candidate_facts_list.fact: dbt determines whether grants are 'carried over' for incremental models based on materialization and the target database
candidate_facts_list.quote: It knows whether grants are “carried over” when a model is re-run based on its materialization and your database.

candidate_facts_list.fact: dbt does not treat schemas as first-class configurable objects; schema USAGE grants must still be applied via hooks
candidate_facts_list.quote:
there isn’t really a way to configure *schemas as their own objects* within dbt.
For now, it’s still necessary to grant `usage` on schemas

candidate_facts_list.fact: The 'manage grants' capability is global — users with the transformer role can change grants on any object as if they were the owner
candidate_facts_list.quote: It is worth noting that this privilege *is* a global privilege – now anyone using the `transformer` role can change grants on any object as though they are the owner of the object.

candidate_facts_list.fact: Database-specific advanced permissions (Snowflake row access policies, masking) still require post-hooks to apply
candidate_facts_list.quote: in Snowflake, you’ll still want a `post-hook` to apply a [row access policy] or a column [masking policy] to your table

candidate_facts_list.fact: `grants` config is exposed via dbt metadata/graph, allowing macros to iterate graph.nodes to infer schema-level grants
candidate_facts_list.quote: Now that `grants` is a real config in dbt, available via dbt metadata, you can do all sorts of fun things with it. For instance, figure out which schemas have at least one object granting `select` to a role

candidate_facts_list.fact: Set folder-level materializations in dbt_project.yml to materialize all models in a folder as tables, avoiding per-model 'materialized: view'.
candidate_facts_list.quote: If all of your models in a folder are tables, define the materialization on the dbt_project.yml file rather than on the model file.

candidate_facts_list.fact: dbt models default to materialization 'view' — you do not need to declare models as views explicitly.
candidate_facts_list.quote: By default, dbt models are materialized as “views”. This removes the need to declare any models as views.

candidate_facts_list.fact: Use post-hooks to grant permissions to other transformers and BI users so model changes remain accessible to collaborators.
candidate_facts_list.quote: Do you use post-hooks to grant permissions to other transformers and BI users? ... This will ensure that any changes made will be accessible to your collaborators

candidate_facts_list.fact: Prefer folder selectors or YAML selectors over tagging every model; majority of models should remain untagged.
candidate_facts_list.quote: The majority of your project’s models should be untagged. ... you can use folder selectors in many cases to eliminate over tagging of every model in a folder.

candidate_facts_list.fact: YAML selectors enable intricate, layered model selection and can replace complicated tagging schemes.
candidate_facts_list.quote: Are you using YAML selectors? These enable intricate, layered model selection and can eliminate complicated tagging mechanisms

candidate_facts_list.fact: Install the dbt_utils package to reuse community macros (no need to copy macros into your project).
candidate_facts_list.quote: Do you have the dbt_utils package installed? This is by far our most popular and essential package. ... you have access to the macros (no need to copy them over to your project).

candidate_facts_list.fact: Incremental models MUST use unique keys and the is_incremental() macro to implement correct incremental logic.
candidate_facts_list.quote: If you have incremental models, are they using unique keys and is_incremental() macro?

candidate_facts_list.fact: In dbt Cloud, configure jobs to inherit from the environment to make upgrading dbt versions easier.
candidate_facts_list.quote: What dbt version are the jobs? Are the majority of them inheriting from the environment to make upgrading easier?

candidate_facts_list.fact: All sources should have corresponding staging models to clean/standardize structure; avoid direct joins between sources or into intermediates.
candidate_facts_list.quote: All sources should have a corresponding staging model to clean and standardize the data structure. They should not look like the image below.

candidate_facts_list.fact: dbt Codegen macro generate_model_yaml requires model_names and supports upstream_descriptions (default=False).
candidate_facts_list.quote:
* `model_names` (required): The model(s) you wish to generate YAML for.
* `upstream_descriptions` (optional, `default=False`): Whether you want to include descriptions for identical column names from upstream models.

candidate_facts_list.fact: generate_model_yaml accepts multiple model_names in one call to output a single combined .yml for several models.
candidate_facts_list.quote: $ dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml --args '{{"model_names": [ "activity_based_interest_activated", "activity_based_interest_deactivated", "activity_based_interest_updated", ...] }}'

candidate_facts_list.fact: Use dbt ls -m <path> --output name to programmatically list model names for piping into generate_model_yaml.
candidate_facts_list.quote: $ dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name | xargs -I{{}} echo -n ' "{{}}",'

candidate_facts_list.fact: Run dbt docs generate to validate YAML and surface syntax errors before running dbt docs serve.
candidate_facts_list.quote: Run `dbt docs generate`. If there are syntax errors, this will be found out at this stage.

candidate_facts_list.fact: Create docs blocks with {{% docs <name> %}}...{{% enddocs %}} and reference them in schema YAML via {{ doc('<name>') }}.
candidate_facts_list.quote:
$ cat .../_activity_based_interest_docs.md  {{% docs activity_based_interest__id %}} ... {{% enddocs %}}
$ cat .../_activity_based_interest_docs.yml  ... description: "{{{{ doc('activity_based_interest__id') }}}"

candidate_facts_list.fact: The solution was tested on Mac/VS Code; regex behavior may vary across environments (platform-specific regex caveat).
candidate_facts_list.quote: Note that this solution has been tested on Mac/VS Code, and that regex behavior may vary between stacks.

candidate_facts_list.fact: Extract all unique columns in a folder via: grep '      \- name:' <file> | cut -c 15- | sort -u to produce a deduplicated list.
candidate_facts_list.quote: $ grep '      \\- name:' models/core/activity_based_interest/_activity_based_interest_docs.yml | cut -c 15- | sort -u

candidate_facts_list.fact: When adding models or columns to an existing folder, prefer adding docs/doc-blocks manually rather than programmatic replacements.
candidate_facts_list.quote: When adding additional models to a folder, or additional columns to an existing model, I would suggest adding new documentation and docs blocks manually rather than programmatically.
